messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Welder
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Eighty-year-old Malia came to the clinic at her daughter’s urging, though she would not have come on her own. She sat upright in the chair, hands folded in her lap, her welding-scarred forearms visible beneath the rolled sleeves of her flannel shirt. She had been a welder for forty-seven years, and her body showed it—the calluses, the slight tremor in her left hand from decades of holding a torch, the hearing loss in her right ear. But what troubled her now was not the ordinary wear of a working life. She believed, with a certainty that had calcified over the years, that her body had been permanently damaged by what happened, and that she would never feel normal emotions again.

The event itself had occurred fifty-three years ago, when Malia was twenty-seven and newly married to a man she had met at a community dance in Honolulu. He was charming at first, then possessive, then violent. The worst night came after she told him she wanted to leave. He pinned her to the kitchen floor, his knee on her sternum, and beat her until she lost consciousness. She woke hours later, alone, with three cracked ribs, a dislocated shoulder, and blood in her urine. She did not go to the hospital. She did not call the police. She cleaned herself up, told her coworkers she had fallen down stairs, and stayed. She stayed for eleven more years, until he left her for someone else.

Now, in her old age, Malia lived with her second husband, a gentle man named Keoni who had never raised a hand to her. But she could not feel safe in her own home. She slept in brief, fitful stretches, waking several times each night to check the locks, to peer down the hallway, to listen for footsteps that were not there. She had come to believe that her body was unreliable—that it could not be trusted to protect her, that it had failed her that night and would fail her again. She no longer trusted her own physical sensations. A sudden tightness in her chest, a creak in the floorboards, the weight of a hand on her shoulder from behind—each sent a spike of cold alert through her, and she would freeze, scanning the room for threat.

Her work as a welder had once been a source of pride and focus. She had been one of the first women in her union, and she had built bridges and ships and scaffolding that still stood. But now, the welding shop triggered her constantly. The hiss of the torch sounded like the sharp intake of breath before a blow. The clatter of a dropped tool on concrete made her flinch so hard she once burned her forearm. The smell of hot metal brought her back to the kitchen floor, to the smell of her own blood on the linoleum. She had begun to avoid certain jobs—anything that required her to work on the ground, anything that required her to be alone in a confined space. Her foreman had noticed and had moved her to lighter tasks, but the shame of it sat heavy in her chest. She had been a master welder; now she was afraid of a dropped wrench.

The consequence that finally brought her to seek help was relational. Her granddaughter, who lived nearby, had stopped visiting. Malia had snapped at her one afternoon when the girl came up behind her and touched her shoulder to say hello. Malia had spun around, grabbed the girl’s wrist, and shouted. Her granddaughter was fourteen and had cried. Malia had not been able to apologize properly—she had stood there, stiff and silent, because she could not find the words. She had come to believe that she would never feel normal emotions again, that something inside her had been broken and not repaired. She could not cry at her granddaughter’s tears. She could not feel the warmth of Keoni’s hand on her back without wanting to pull away. She was trapped inside a body she no longer trusted, inside a home that felt like a battleground, inside a life that had been shaped by a single night fifty-three years ago.

What frightened her most, she said, was the possibility that this was simply who she was now. That the hypervigilance, the sleeplessness, the numbness, the mistrust of her own flesh—these were not symptoms of something that could be healed, but the permanent architecture of an old woman who had been broken too long ago. She came to the clinic not because she believed she could change, but because her daughter had begged her, and because she was afraid of losing her granddaughter forever. She hoped, faintly and without conviction, that maybe there was a way to feel safe inside her own skin again, even if she could not imagine what that would feel like.
